items.alt: The road running on beneath the canopy

children.text: A mahogany plantation covering about
2km

of road between Loboc and Bilar in the interior of Bohol. Trees planted half a century ago to restore bare hills have grown until their branches meet above the road, and today it is a green tunnel that Bohol countryside tours stop at without fail.
Bilar Man-Made Forest lies on the Loay Interior Road in Bohol's central uplands, along the boundary between the towns of Loboc and Bilar. Over a stretch of about
2km

, tall mahogany trees stand close together on both sides of the road, and their high branches touch overhead, forming a cool green tunnel even at midday. The Bohol Provincial Tourism Office describes it as a forest of mainly white and red mahogany, the result of a reforestation program that began more than half a century ago.

This forest was not originally natural. Logging continued in Bohol from colonial times, leaving hills across the island bare, and soil was often washed away when it rained. So mahogany seedlings, native to Central and South America, were planted in rows on the slopes, and those trees have grown for decades into what you see today. The thick roots exposed on the roadside slopes, holding the soil in place, silently show why they were planted.

However, a forest planted densely with a single foreign species has ecological drawbacks. The travel site Wikivoyage notes that native birds can hardly live here and that only some kinds of insects have increased, and says the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) is gradually changing the single-species forest by planting native trees in the understory. So the forest is both a beautiful landscape and an open-air classroom where you can see the gains and losses of reforestation in one place.
By location, the forest is described as lying inside the Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape. The protected landscape, Bohol's largest tract of natural forest, was designated a national park in
and redesignated as a protected landscape in
. Most travelers stop here for about
30 minutes to 1 hour

during a countryside tour to take photos and move on, but if you have time you can combine the nearby spring and the protected landscape's trails and spend half a day in Bilar. It is not a hard place to walk, so it is no burden for family trips or trips with parents.

blocks.title: Passing slowly through the mahogany tunnel

children.text: The heart of the forest is driving slowly through the roughly
2km

stretch. With the windows down at low speed, you can feel the shade and the drop in temperature made by the branches overlapping above the road. In the middle of the forest the road winds, and the way light pours through the trees keeps changing.

Stand at the roadside and look up, and straight trunks, tangled branches and the sky between them all fit into one frame. A wide-angle lens or your phone's wide mode gives a good composition with the trunks converging to a point. The slanting light of morning and late afternoon brings out the texture of the trunks better than the direct sun of midday.

blocks.title: A walk along the roadside shoulder

children.text: The forest stretch is nice to explore on foot. Walking along the edge of the road, you can see up close the roots exposed on the slopes, the smooth trunks and the fallen leaves on the ground. But vehicles keep passing, so walk only on the inner side of the shoulder and take special care on the curves.

Look closely at the trunks and almost every tree has the same form. They are about the same height, the bark splits in straight lines, and there is little grass or brush on the ground, which gives a bare feeling. Seeing with your own eyes how simple the layers of this forest are compared with natural forest helps you understand why it differs from the natural forest of the protected landscape.

blocks.title: The quiet forest in early morning

children.text: If you come early in the morning, avoiding the hours when tour vehicles crowd in, there are hardly any people on the road. Birdsong and insect sounds carry well, and the light on dew-covered leaves is at its softest. It is the best time for anyone who wants to take photos slowly or go jogging or walking.

The protected landscape area deeper in Bilar has springs including Logarita, and Logarita Spring is built up like a swimming pool where you can soak in cool spring water. It is a good place to stop next when the heat rises after taking photos in the forest. Facilities such as benches and restrooms are said to be available around the spring.

blocks.title: Trekking and birdwatching in Rajah Sikatuna

children.text: The protected landscape has marked trails running more than
30km
, and it is regarded as Bohol's best birdwatching site, with more than
120 species

of birds recorded. From the observation tower on Bilar Peak you can look down over the surrounding hills. Unlike the monotonous plantation you saw along the forest road, here you meet the varied natural forest of limestone country, and the contrast is clear when you see the two in sequence.

items.title: Early-morning forest stop
items.subtitle: About 1 hour with a private or chartered vehicle

children.text: Set out by vehicle from your accommodation in Panglao or Tagbilaran. Bring snacks and water.
Pass Loboc and climb the steep curves to the entrance of the forest stretch. Park at a safe shoulder or parking space.
Walk along the shoulder and take looking-up photos and photos of the winding road. It is early, so tour-group vehicles are still few.
Drive on through the whole forest and take in the view from the opposite side once more.
Continue toward the Chocolate Hills, or turn off toward Logarita Spring deeper in Bilar.

This itinerary focuses on the forest itself. Even if you add the Chocolate Hills there is plenty of time, and since tour vehicles usually move in the direction that climbs up from Loboc, going in the order that comes down from the Bilar side may sometimes mean fewer people.

items.title: Bilar half-day itinerary
items.subtitle: A route mixing public transport and habal-habal to reach deeper into Bilar

children.text: Take a bus or van toward Carmen or Bilar from the Dao Integrated Bus Terminal in Tagbilaran.
Tell the driver in advance and get off at the forest stretch. Walk along the edge of the road and look around for about
40 minutes
Head toward Bilar town. Use a habal-habal motorcycle taxi or a passing vehicle.
Register at the entrance to the Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape and walk a nearby trail, or rest at Logarita Spring.
Have lunch at a restaurant in Bilar town. Choices are not many, so keep it simple with local food.
Take a bus again toward Carmen or Tagbilaran. Services thin out later in the afternoon, so don't leave it late.

This itinerary depends on transport timings working out. If you are not sure about a ride back, it is safer to get the contact number of a habal-habal driver or a charter vehicle from your accommodation in advance.
It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG) on a direct flight. The airport is on Panglao Island, about
36km
from the forest in a straight line, and by car you should allow about
1.5–2 hours
. There are also direct flights from Incheon to Bohol, but airlines and operating days vary by season, so check before booking.
Fast craft run from Cebu to Tagbilaran Port and take about
2 hours
. Tagbilaran is Bohol's gateway city, and from the port to the forest is about
1 hour
by car. Even if you come from Manila or Cebu on a day trip, it is usual to arrange a vehicle in Tagbilaran.
A bus or van from the Dao Integrated Bus Terminal in Tagbilaran toward Bilar or Carmen takes about
1 to 1.5 hours
, and the fare is about
. If you want to get off in front of the forest, tell the driver or conductor when you board. Return services can thin out late in the afternoon, so check the last departure in advance.
The most comfortable option is to charter a van or car for the day and do the countryside tour. A day's charter of one vehicle runs roughly

, and entrance fees and meals are often extra. Some travelers rent a motorbike in Panglao and ride up, but the mountain road has many climbs and sharp curves, so it is recommended only if you have plenty of riding experience.
From Loboc town to the forest is about
20 minutes
by car, and from the forest to Bilar town is about
5km
in a straight line. The road to the protected landscape entrance goes another
8km
in from the junction on the Loay Interior Road. For stretches that public transport does not reach, a habal-habal is the most realistic choice.

The forest itself stays green year-round, so the scenery does not change much with the seasons. What matters more is how the weather affects walking and photography. In Bohol, the northeast monsoon blows from
November–April
, bringing mostly cool, clear days, with an average daytime temperature of about
May–July
sees temperature and humidity rise together, and in
August–October
the southwest monsoon makes the weather changeable, with fine days and rainy days alternating.

Right after rain the forest is at its deepest green and moss and ferns come alive, so photos are crisp, but the road is wet and slippery and leaves and twigs pile up. Bohol lies south of the typhoon track and is less affected than Luzon, but some years have brought heavy damage, such as Typhoon Odette in
December 2021
. From late autumn to early in the year, check typhoon forecasts and road conditions before and after your trip.

items.label: Simple lunch
items.note: At restaurants in Bilar and Loboc towns

children.text: Prices are approximate as of 2026 and may vary depending on local conditions.
There are not many places to stay near the forest, so most travelers stay on Panglao Island around Alona Beach or in Tagbilaran city and visit as a day trip. Resorts on Panglao cost
and up per night, and hotels in Tagbilaran city run about

. If you want a quiet countryside feel, another option is to spend a night at a small lodging by the Loboc River or on the Bilar side and walk the forest early in the morning. In that case, confirm in advance whether the lodging is operating and how to book.

There are not many restaurants right in front of the forest, so think of it as a place to get just simple snacks and drinks. Lunch is often had at the Loboc River floating buffet or at restaurants in Bilar and Loboc towns. Bohol specialty snacks include calamay, a chewy rice sweet served in coconut shells, piaya, a thin sweet flatbread, and ube dessert made from purple yam, and many people buy them as souvenirs.
The hours when tour vehicles crowd in are said to be around
9 AM–12 PM
. Go before
8 AM
or after
2 PM
and you can take photos in much more peace.
Don't just watch the scenery from the car window; get out and walk at least once. The temperature and smell of the air in the shade are completely different from inside the car.
Looking-up photos tend to make the trunks look tilted, so hold your phone level and use the central trunk as your reference for a steady shot.
There may be mosquitoes and small insects in the forest shade, so bring repellent, and wear shoes that don't slip after rain.
Commercial and event shoots such as pre-wedding photos are said to need cooperation from the local government. For a sizable shoot, inquire in advance with the Bilar tourism office.
When booking a countryside tour, ask the driver how long you will stay at the forest. If the schedule is tight, some tours leave after as little as
10 minutes
Because this is a protected landscape, drone flying may be subject to rules. Check on-site notices and the latest announcements before flying.
Bring plenty of cash. There may be no ATM nearby, and many habal-habal drivers and snack sellers accept cash only.
The forest stretch is an actual road with traffic. Standing in the middle of the road to take photos risks a collision with a car coming around a curve, so never do it.
The road bends and sight lines are short, so drivers notice people late. When taking photos, always stand on the inner side of the shoulder and have a companion watch for vehicles.

Whether visitor fees and environmental charges are collected has changed over the years by decision of the protected-area management. Before going, check the latest notice from the Bohol Provincial Tourism Office or the Bilar local government.
Do not scribble on the trees, break branches or leave trash. This is a plantation within the protected landscape, and work to replace the forest by planting native species is said to be under way.
After rain, leaves and soil can wash from the slopes onto the road, and branches can fall in strong wind. Check the state of the road right after a typhoon.
In front of the forest, facilities such as restrooms and a large parking area may not be sufficient. Use the restroom before you travel, and take your trash with you.
About
40 minutes to 1 hour
by car east toward Carmen, Bohol's signature scene of countless cone-shaped hills seen from a viewpoint.
Heading west down from the forest, Loboc town is about
20 minutes
by car, and the floating buffet cruise on the river is the lunch stop of the countryside tour.
About
1 hour
by car to Corella, where you can see the palm-sized Philippine tarsier up close.
Heading down toward Tagbilaran, it is about
1 hour
by car, and you can see one of the oldest stone churches in Bohol.
About
8km
in from the road junction, Bohol's largest tract of natural forest with trails, springs and birdwatching.
